label: Knots and Links, Reidemeister Moves
notes: Open the course. Knot theory studies circles embedded in three-dimensional space up to continuous deformation. The lecture follows printed pages 1 through 10 and introduces knots and links, the diagrams that picture them on paper, and the three Reidemeister moves that capture exactly when two diagrams represent the same knot.

label: Knots and Links
notes: Define a knot as a smooth embedding of a circle into three-space, and a link as several disjoint circles tangled together. The unknot is the trivial circle, and the central question is to decide when a complicated-looking knot is secretly trivial. Examples like the trefoil and the Hopf link anchor the whole subject.

label: Knot Diagrams
notes: Project a knot onto a plane to get a diagram, a curve with finitely many transverse crossings, each marked to show which strand passes over. Diagrams turn a spatial problem into a combinatorial one on paper. Almost all of knot theory is carried out by manipulating these pictures rather than the embeddings themselves.

label: The Reidemeister Moves
notes: Introduce the three local moves: a twist, a poke, and a slide. Reidemeister's theorem says two diagrams represent the same knot exactly when one can be turned into the other by a finite sequence of these moves plus planar isotopy. This reduces equivalence of knots to a finite local calculus.

label: Invariants from Moves
notes: Explain the strategy that drives the course. To prove two knots are different, attach a quantity to a diagram that is unchanged by all three Reidemeister moves; such a knot invariant then depends only on the knot. Checking invariance move by move is the recurring method behind every invariant we build.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. Knots and links are embedded circles studied up to deformation, diagrams record them combinatorially with over and under crossings, and the three Reidemeister moves generate all equivalences. Quantities invariant under these moves are knot invariants, and the next lecture builds the first powerful one, the Conway polynomial.
